Verify with a paper exercise (completely fictional, containing no real equipment parameters or unit information): you are given a subunit training and equipment maintenance task package (training subjects and assessment standards, equipment and ammunition and material lists, personnel and duty and rotation arrangements, safety and confidentiality requirements, and one training accident or equipment failure or disciplinary incident). The task is to rank the shift priorities according to the chain of command and safety rules, explain how training organization, equipment maintenance, safety supervision, and anomaly reporting connect, and write out the required checklists, command and review points, record and handover formats, and the actions that must be reported when beyond one's own authority.

Signals more worth considering: willingness to lead a subunit in a strict discipline and high-risk training environment, the ability to organize training and equipment maintenance according to superior intent and safety rules, and the ability to maintain judgment and execution under pressure. Signals to be cautious about: unwillingness to accept strict hierarchy and confidentiality constraints; difficulty with high-intensity physical fitness and field and rotating duty; imagining this kind of work as relying only on personal bravery. Self-check with the paper exercise on this page, rather than drawing conclusions from personality labels.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute a hiring, competency scoring, or military appointment conclusion.

First judge whether you are willing to make front-line military leadership a long-term career: it requires leading a subunit within the chain of command, bearing training and equipment and personnel and safety responsibility, organizing actions according to doctrine and superior intent, and being accountable for results; verify this with the paper exercise on this page.

The work of this occupation unfolds around the cycle of 'receiving the mission and assessing the situation — developing the subunit plan and division of labor — organizing training and equipment maintenance — executing guard and fire and maneuver tasks and organizing firepower and coordination — supervising discipline and safety and handling anomalies — reporting and after-action review': within the chain of command, translate superior intent into executable subunit tasks, arrange shifts and division of labor, organize training and assessment, verify equipment and ammunition and materials, supervise safety and discipline, and report anomalies according to procedures.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the US SOC/O*NET 55-2012.00 'First-Line Supervisors of Weapons Specialists/Crew Members' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'First-Line Supervisors (Weapons Specialists / Crew Members)'): supervise and coordinate the activities of weapons specialists / crew members; supervisors may also perform the same activities as the personnel they supervise. Example job titles include Armor Senior Sergeant, Field Artillery Senior Sergeant and Infantry Unit Leader. This occupation is a military occupation, and O*NET explicitly states that it does not collect military occupation data, so there is no official task list and no wage and employment statistics.
entries.question: What do first-line supervisors of weapons specialists / crew members mainly do?

entries.answer: The focus of responsibility and the outputs differ: this occupation is a military occupation, and its output is leading subunits within the chain of command and supervising weapons specialists / crew members in training and operations; security first-line supervisors output access control and patrol and incident handling and security team supervision at employer sites; police and detective first-line supervisors output patrol and investigation and case handling under civilian law enforcement authority; correctional officer first-line supervisors output correctional custody and order among detainees; firefighting and prevention worker first-line supervisors output firefighting and rescue and fireground command; safety management specialists and security managers output corporate safety programmes and operations. This occupation does not include civilian law enforcement or correctional custody authority, nor employer site security positions.
entries.question: How is it different from security first-line supervisors and police and corrections first-line supervisors?

entries.answer: US SOC/O*NET 55-2012.00 is a military occupation. O*NET explicitly states that it does not collect military occupation data, so there are no task, work activity, work context, interest code and Job Zone and education statistics for this occupation; the BLS OEWS and employment projections likewise do not cover military occupations, so there is no wage percentile, employment size, growth or openings data for this occupation. The US part of this page uses the Department of Defense 2026 basic pay table to explain the compensation structure by rank and years of service (E-5 about 3,342.90 to 4,421.70 US dollars / month, E-6 about 3,401.10 to 5,267.70 US dollars / month, E-7 about 3,932.10 to 6,245.70 US dollars / month, excluding allowances and subsidies), and does not provide an occupational wage median or employment projections.

entries.answer: This occupation is a military occupation and O*NET does not collect work context and preparation level data for it, so this page does not provide O*NET work context percentages and Job Zone. The public definition only states that it is a first-line military supervisor who supervises and coordinates weapons specialists / crew members and may also perform the same tasks personally. Enlistment and training and assignment and promotion conditions (age, medical examination, physical fitness, background check, education, specialty assignment selection) are subject to the regulations of your service branch and the competent authority.

entries.answer: A more accurate judgement is that clerical steps such as organising training and assessment ledgers, summarising equipment maintenance and duty records, and drafting reports and notices and training materials will be assisted by tools, while authorisation to use force, operational command, equipment and accident disposition, and discipline and security and promotion remain with the chain of command. The ILO 2023 study focuses mainly on civilian occupations and shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations and that technical feasibility does not equal institutional adoption; the tasks of military occupations are defined by doctrine and the chain of command, and public research is insufficient to give adoption rates or position changes for this occupation, so the conclusion is that clerical methods will change, not that the occupation will be wholly replaced.
